strengths: The proposed AAD rule is simple, practical, and easy to integrate when both the DPO model and its SFT reference are available: decode among plausible DPO tokens using the DPO/SFT log-likelihood ratio.
The paper gives a clear motivation connecting KL-regularized preference optimization to residual SFT bias, and the method is intuitively related to using the DPO model as an implicit token reward.

Empirical coverage is fairly broad: multiple preference datasets, two model families and several model sizes, comparisons to greedy DPO/SFT, best-of-2, and an EFT-style baseline, plus some data-scarcity and iterative-DPO experiments.

The results are directionally promising: AAD often substantially improves oracle reward and pairwise win rate, and the synthetic-data experiment suggests a potentially useful training-time application.
weaknesses: The central empirical evidence relies heavily on reward-model scores, often from reward models trained on the same preference dataset distribution used to train the aligned models. This supports reward-model optimization, but only weakly establishes improved human alignment or safety. AlpacaEval results help, but are reported only as AAD win rates against baselines and are limited to some settings.

The method is quite close to contrastive/logit-difference decoding using an aligned model and reference model. The paper does not sufficiently distinguish AAD from prior contrastive decoding, proxy alignment, EFT, DeRa, and reward-guided decoding beyond implementation details, so the originality is incremental.

There are technical and presentation issues in the derivation. Eq. 5 appears to have a malformed ratio involving log pi_SFT in the denominator, and the text defining r_DPO omits the logarithm before later using a log-ratio token score. These errors do not necessarily invalidate the algorithm, but they weaken confidence in the theoretical presentation.

The claim of compute-equivalent evaluation is not fully substantiated. AAD requires two model forward passes per token, while best-of-N also involves sampling and reward-model scoring; the paper does not provide wall-clock, memory, batching, or latency comparisons, despite efficiency being part of the motivation.

The hyperparameter behavior is underexplored. The main method fixes alpha=0.1, while beam experiments use alpha=0.7 and introduce an entropy threshold; there is no systematic ablation of alpha, beta, thresholding, sequence length, decoding temperature, or robustness across prompt types.

The iterative-DPO/synthetic-data claim is interesting but not yet convincing: controls are limited, the rejected samples are generated by nucleus sampling from pi_DPO, and it is unclear whether gains come from AAD specifically, extra DPO training, distributional self-training effects, or reward-model overfitting.

Reproducibility is inadequate in the submitted manuscript: Appendix A.6 says the source code can be accessed at a link, but the rendered page contains no link. Dataset splits, exact prompt counts, random seeds, evaluation sample sizes, and model/checkpoint identifiers are also insufficiently specified for reliable reproduction.

Limitations and ethics are only lightly treated. The paper notes the two-forward-pass cost and need for access to the SFT model, but does not discuss safety failure modes, reward hacking at inference, possible amplification of reward-model biases, or risks from using AAD-generated synthetic preference data.

strengths: The core idea is simple and potentially useful: decode from a DPO model using the DPO/SFT log-probability ratio over a plausibility-filtered token set. It is easy to understand, uses models already present in a standard DPO pipeline, and addresses a real limitation of ordinary DPO decoding.

The paper evaluates across several preference datasets and multiple model families/sizes, and the reported reward-model scores are consistently favorable to AAD. The comparison to best-of-N at different N is a useful attempt to contextualize inference cost.
The manuscript includes some practical analysis beyond the main table, including data-scarcity experiments, beta sensitivity, beam-search variants, and an iterative-DPO synthetic data use case.
weaknesses: The central empirical evidence is not fully convincing because evaluation relies heavily on reward models as oracles. This risks measuring optimization of reward-model preferences rather than true alignment, helpfulness, or safety. The paper lacks human evaluation or stronger external task-based evaluation sufficient to support broad alignment claims.

The baselines are too limited for the claims. The paper discusses many inference-time alignment methods but mainly compares against greedy decoding, best-of-2, and one EFT variant. There is no direct comparison to stronger reward-guided decoding/search methods such as ARGS, DeAl, controlled/reward-augmented decoding, PAD, or value-guided methods under matched budgets.

The theoretical justification is informal and overclaimed. The derivation shows that KL-regularized policies inherit SFT likelihood bias, but it does not establish that greedy tokenwise maximization of the DPO/SFT log ratio over an alpha-filtered set reliably optimizes sequence-level reward. The method is plausible, but the paper presents it as more theoretically grounded than demonstrated.

Several experimental details needed for reproducibility are missing or underspecified: sample counts for evaluation prompts, random seeds, decoding length limits, exact model checkpoints, hardware/inference cost accounting, code link contents, and hyperparameter selection procedures. Section A.6 appears to promise a code link but the extracted manuscript provides no usable URL.

The compute-equivalent framing is weak. AAD requires two forward passes per generated token and access to the SFT model; best-of-2 and other baselines may have different sequence lengths and batching behavior. The paper does not provide wall-clock latency, FLOPs, memory, or throughput measurements.

The synthetic-data/iterative-DPO claim is not adequately isolated. AAD-generated outputs are labeled as chosen and nucleus samples as rejected, then evaluated primarily by reward models. This could amplify the same reward-model biases and does not demonstrate that the resulting model improves under independent human or safety evaluation.

Presentation quality has multiple issues that reduce confidence: the related-work section appears to end mid-sentence, there are typos such as “againgst,” “Agrilla,” “helpfullness,” and “traind,” and some equations/text are inconsistent or unclear, including the reward ratio/log-ratio description.

The qualitative examples are weak evidence. Some best-of-2 outputs are identical or nearly identical to AAD, yet the captions still claim AAD demonstrates superior structured reasoning or contextual sensitivity. The examples often reward verbosity rather than clearly better alignment.

Limitations and ethics are underdeveloped. The paper only briefly notes the need for two forward passes and SFT-model access. It does not seriously discuss reward-model bias, safety failure modes, over-refusal or verbosity, misuse of synthetic preference data, privacy/licensing of datasets, or the risk of amplifying harmful preference signals.

strengths: The paper proposes a simple and appealing inference-time alignment method: use the DPO model/reference-model log-likelihood ratio as a token-level alignment reward, constrained by plausibility filtering. The method is easy to understand, requires no extra training beyond an existing DPO setup, and connects naturally to the interpretation of DPO models as implicit reward/Q functions.

The empirical results are broad and encouraging. AAD is evaluated across several preference datasets, multiple model families and sizes, LoRA and full fine-tuning settings, and both internally trained and external reward models. The gains over greedy DPO, greedy SFT, best-of-2, and an EFT-style baseline are usually consistent and sometimes large.

The paper includes useful secondary analyses: comparison to best-of-N at varying N, low-data behavior, sensitivity to DPO beta, beam-search variants, AlpacaEval-style evaluation, and iterative DPO using AAD-generated synthetic chosen responses. These experiments make the method feel practically relevant rather than just a decoding trick.

The presentation is mostly clear. The motivation from KL-constrained preference optimization is well explained, and the method itself is concise enough that readers could implement it from the equations and decoding description.

The limitations that are discussed are real and relevant: AAD needs access to the SFT/reference model and roughly doubles per-token forward-pass cost. The paper does not oversell the method as free at inference time.
weaknesses: The evaluation relies heavily on reward-model scores, often with reward models trained from the same preference data distribution used to train the DPO model. This is a reasonable proxy, but it leaves open whether the large gains translate to human preference, safety, factuality, or robustness outside the reward model's biases. The AlpacaEval results help, but the paper would be stronger with direct human evaluation or more independent LLM-judge protocols.

The novelty is useful but somewhat incremental. The ingredients are close to contrastive decoding, DPO-as-reward interpretations, emulated fine-tuning/proxy alignment, and reward-guided decoding. The main contribution is a clean recombination and empirical demonstration rather than a fundamentally new alignment objective or theory.

Reproducibility is only partial. Hyperparameters are reported, but sample sizes, prompt formatting details, decoding length settings, exact model checkpoints, alpha tuning protocol, and evaluation scripts are not fully specified in the main text. The appendix section on code and models appears to end with “can be accessed at:” but no visible link, which is a material issue for reproducibility.

The baselines could be stronger. Best-of-2 is compute-comparable, but the paper does not fully compare against recent inference-time alignment/search methods under carefully matched latency and memory budgets. Some claims about compute equivalence are also underspecified because AAD uses two forward passes per generated token, while BoN methods have different batching and reward-scoring costs.

There is limited analysis of failure modes. Since AAD maximizes a ratio, even with plausibility filtering it may overemphasize tokens that changed under DPO for idiosyncratic reasons, and the paper does not deeply analyze degradation cases, calibration, diversity loss, verbosity, or harmful behavior under adversarial prompts.

The manuscript has several presentation issues that should be fixed: typographical errors such as “againgst,” “with with,” and “traind,” inconsistent spelling of Argilla/Agrilla, an unfinished related-work sentence, and some equations/typesetting that obscure the intended log-ratio reward. These do not undermine the main idea, but they reduce polish.

strengths: The core idea is simple, technically motivated, and practically useful: decoding with a DPO/SFT log-probability ratio over a plausibility-filtered token set is an appealing inference-time way to reuse preference information without additional training or an external reward model.

The paper gives a reasonable theoretical connection to KL-regularized preference optimization and Q/advantage-style token scoring, while also acknowledging the need for min-alpha filtering to avoid degenerate ratio maximization.

The empirical section is broad: results cover several preference datasets, Llama and Qwen scales, LoRA and full fine-tuning, open-source OLMo DPO checkpoints, AlpacaEval-style judging, data-scaling, beta sensitivity, beam-search variants, throughput, and iterative DPO use.
The method appears especially useful in low-data settings and as a synthetic preference-data generator; the iterative DPO experiments are a promising secondary contribution.
Presentation is generally clear, with a concise algorithm and enough high-level training hyperparameters to understand the experimental setup.
weaknesses: The central empirical evidence relies heavily on reward-model evaluation, often with oracle reward models trained on the same preference data distribution used to train the DPO model. Since AAD explicitly exploits the DPO/SFT reward signal, the reward-model gains may partly reflect evaluator alignment or reward-model overoptimization rather than robust human preference improvement.

The human evaluation is helpful but too narrow to fully validate the broad alignment claims: it covers one model/dataset setting, 502 pairwise judgments, and does not appear to analyze annotator agreement, prompt categories, length effects, or safety-specific behavior.

Potential length and verbosity confounding is not adequately addressed. AAD examples often produce longer, more explanatory completions, and reward models and LLM judges can favor verbosity; the paper does not report output lengths, length-normalized rewards, or controlled comparisons.

The theoretical justification motivates the token ratio, but the actual greedy, min-alpha-filtered decoding rule remains heuristic. The paper does not provide guarantees that local token-ratio maximization improves sequence-level reward, nor does it deeply characterize failure modes when the DPO/SFT ratio is miscalibrated.

Baselines are somewhat limited for an inference-time alignment paper. The main comparisons are greedy, Bo2, EFT, contrastive decoding, and beam search; stronger recent reward-guided or value-guided decoding methods discussed in related work are not empirically compared under matched budgets.

Reproducibility is weakened by the apparent missing/blank code link: the manuscript says code is available and Section A.5 points to source code, but no actual URL is present in the extracted paper. Important implementation details such as exact prompt counts for all tables, decoding max lengths, stopping criteria beyond the user token, seeds, and statistical uncertainty are also incomplete.

Limitations and ethics are present but fairly generic. The paper notes misuse risks and PPO inconsistency, but does not thoroughly discuss cases where AAD may amplify biases in the preference data, enforce undesirable preferences, or degrade factuality/safety despite higher reward scores.

strengths: The core idea is simple and practically appealing: decode using the DPO/SFT log-probability ratio restricted to plausible tokens under the DPO model. This is easy to implement when both checkpoints are available and avoids training an additional reward model at inference time.

The paper evaluates across several preference datasets, model families, and scales, and includes useful ablations on alpha, DPO beta, data scaling, full fine-tuning, beam search, and iterative DPO. The reported reward-model gains are large and consistent in many tables.

The authors acknowledge several real limitations, including the need for two forward passes per token, access to the original SFT model, and weaker applicability outside the SFT+DPO setting, with PPO results showing mixed behavior.
The manuscript is generally readable and well structured, with clear pseudocode and a reasonable connection to prior work on DPO, contrastive decoding, and inference-time alignment.
weaknesses: The central empirical evidence relies heavily on reward-model evaluation, often with reward models trained on closely related data distributions. Since AAD explicitly maximizes a DPO/SFT log-ratio that is itself motivated as a reward proxy, the large oracle-reward improvements may partly reflect evaluator alignment or reward-model overoptimization rather than genuine human preference gains.

The human evaluation is too limited to validate the broad claims: only 502 pairwise judgments, one model family, one dataset, and sparse details on prompt sampling, rater instructions, blinding, inter-annotator agreement, confidence intervals, and statistical significance. This is not enough support for claims of consistent alignment improvement across settings.

Originality is modest. The method is essentially a contrastive/logit-difference decoding rule with a plausibility constraint, closely related to contrastive decoding, DExperts-style steering, proxy tuning/EFT, and the known DPO-as-reward interpretation. The paper does not clearly isolate what is conceptually new beyond applying this recipe to the DPO/SFT pair.

The theoretical justification is suggestive rather than conclusive. The derivation motivates the log-ratio as a shaped token-level signal, but it does not establish that greedy token-wise maximization under the alpha filter optimizes sequence-level preference reward or avoids known failures of local decoding. Several strong claims about implicit reward optimization are therefore overstated.

The baseline comparison is incomplete for an inference-time alignment paper. Stronger or more directly comparable decoding-time methods using reward guidance, value guidance, DExperts-style decoding, and tuned contrastive baselines are not evaluated thoroughly; EFT is represented by one beta choice, and the fairness of compute-equivalent comparisons is not fully demonstrated.

Reproducibility is weak in important places. The manuscript contains a blank or missing code link, the main evaluation prompt counts are not consistently specified, implementation details for SFT construction and generation length/stopping are incomplete, and uncertainty estimates or multiple random seeds are largely absent.

Presentation overstates the conclusions. Phrases such as “consistently and significantly improves alignment” are stronger than the evidence supports, especially given reward-model dependence, small human evaluation, mixed PPO results, and some appendix cases where gains narrow or reverse.

The ethics and limitations discussion is present but shallow. For a method that can steer outputs according to arbitrary preference signals, the paper should more seriously discuss misuse, bias amplification, evaluator hacking, and cases where optimizing a learned preference signal can reduce truthfulness or diversity.

strengths: The paper proposes a simple and practical inference-time decoding method: select tokens by the DPO/SFT log-probability ratio within a plausibility set under the DPO model. This is technically well motivated by the DPO-as-reward/Q-function view and closely tied to existing preference optimization theory.

Empirical coverage is strong. The method is evaluated across multiple preference datasets, model families/scales, open-source DPO checkpoints, reward-model evaluation, AlpacaEval, and a small human evaluation. The gains over greedy DPO, SFT, Bo2, EFT, contrastive decoding, and beam search are broad and mostly consistent.

The contribution is significant because it offers a lightweight way to improve DPO-aligned models at inference time without training an extra reward model, and it identifies a useful residual alignment signal in the DPO-vs-SFT probability gap.

The paper is generally clear and well organized, with helpful ablations on alpha, data scale, beta, full fine-tuning, beam search, training duration, latency, and iterative DPO. The limitations about needing two forward passes and access to the SFT model are stated honestly.

The synthetic-data/iterative-DPO experiments are a useful extension: they suggest AAD is not only a decoding trick but can also generate preference data that improves standard decoding under low-data settings.
weaknesses: Reproducibility is weaker than expected for an ICML acceptance: the manuscript contains blank placeholders for code availability, and many implementation details that materially affect results are underspecified, including exact prompt counts for most evaluations, random seeds, decoding lengths, sampling temperatures, model checkpoint identifiers, and human-evaluation protocol details.

The central empirical evidence relies heavily on reward models trained from the same preference sources used to train the DPO models. Although Skywork/Nectar external evaluators, AlpacaEval, and human evaluation help, the main tables still risk rewarding optimization toward correlated model-based judges rather than robust human preference improvement.

The theoretical justification is suggestive rather than fully decisive. The log-ratio score includes value-difference terms and AAD greedily maximizes a constrained token-level quantity; the paper does not rigorously establish when this local procedure improves sequence-level human reward or avoids overoptimization beyond the empirical alpha filter.

The human evaluation is encouraging but limited to one dataset/model setting with 502 pairwise judgments. This is not enough to fully validate the strong cross-domain alignment claims, especially because reward-model wins are much larger than human wins.

Originality is moderate rather than exceptional. AAD is a clean and useful synthesis of DPO log-ratio rewards, contrastive decoding/min-alpha filtering, and inference-time alignment, but it is closely related to prior contrastive/EFT/reward-guided decoding work.

Some presentation details reduce confidence: tables occasionally use confusing win-rate definitions or missing entries, Figure 1/qualitative examples are somewhat cherry-pickable, and claims such as compute-equivalent comparison to BoN need more careful accounting because wall-clock, parallelism, and memory costs differ across methods.
